detaileddescription.para: This document describes the runtime architecture of Project Valhalla as it is implemented in src/. It is complementary to README.md, which focuses on installation, configuration and API usage. For generated API reference documentation, run doxygen Doxyfile and open build/docs/doxygen/html/index.html.

sect1.title: 1. System purpose
sect1.para: Valhalla is a C++20 REST service for healthcare scheduling. It exposes a JSON HTTP API under /api/v2 for managing clients (users and providers), services (clinics, pharmacies, laboratories, radiology centres), staff, appointments and clinical records. Requests are authenticated with JWT bearer tokens and authorised against a per-entity permission model; data is persisted in PostgreSQL through Drogon.

listitem.para: HTTP framework: Drogon (event loops, routing, filters/advice, coroutines).
Database: PostgreSQL, accessed either synchronously through libpqxx with a custom connection pool, or asynchronously through Drogon's DbClient (DB_ASYNC=true).
Support libraries: fmt (formatting), jsoncons (JSON), jwt-cpp (tokens), libsodium/cppcodec (password hashing), xxHash (fingerprints), spdlog/Trantor (logging), cURL, ZLIB, c-ares.
Build: CMake + Conan, Catch2 for tests. Dependency versions are pinned in conan.lock.

sect2.title: 3.1 Bootstrap and lifecycle — src/main.cpp, src/server/
sect2.para: main() constructs Server behind a std::unique_ptr and calls run(), converting any escaping std::exception into EXIT_FAILURE. Server::run() prints the banner, conditionally registers the async database client, configures the Drogon application (listener, thread count, log level, custom 404 page), registers two pieces of advice:

listitem.para: Pre-routing advice answers OPTIONS with 204 and rejects non-standard verbs with 405 before any route runs.
Pre-sending advice is the single place CORS headers are written; it runs for every response, including filter-generated and pre-routing replies.

sect2.para: drogon::app().run() blocks until the event loops stop. Shutdown then drains the DbExecutor and PasswordWorker queues before static destruction, in that order, because database tasks may enqueue password work.

sect2.title: 3.2 Configuration — src/configurator/
sect2.para: Configurator owns one EnvLoader-derived settings group per subsystem (server, database, DoS detector, token manager, permission cache, password worker, DB executor, front-end, e-mail sender). Each group's constructor reads its environment variables with defaults declared in defaults.hpp; printValues() logs the effective configuration with secrets redacted. Configurator is itself obtained from the Store.

sect2.title: 3.3 Service registry — src/store/
sect2.para: Store is a thread-safe singleton registry keyed by std::type_index:

listitem.para: getObject<T>() returns the registered instance or lazily constructs one. Construction happens outside the lock to avoid holding the mutex during expensive initialisation, then is re-checked before publication so two concurrent first callers cannot install different instances.
cachedObject<T>() is the request-path variant: a thread_local pointer is reused until a generation counter changes, avoiding a mutex and hash lookup per request.
replaceObject<T>() swaps an instance (used by tests to inject fakes) and increments the generation counter so every thread refreshes its cache.
Registered objects are held as std::shared_ptr<void> and handed out as aliased shared_ptr<T>: ownership is shared, not transferred.

sect2.title: 3.4 Gatekeeper — src/gatekeeper/
sect2.para: GateKeeper is the authentication/authorisation façade. It parses credentials, delegates password verification to PasswordWorker, issues and validates JWTs via TokenManager, tracks sessions in SessionManager, checks per-entity rights in PermissionManager (backed by an idle-expiry PermissionCache), and detects abuse in DOSDetector. Most operations exist in two forms: a callback version used by synchronous controllers and a drogon::Task coroutine version used by asynchronous controllers.

sect2.title: 3.5 Controllers — src/controllers/
sect2.para: EntityControllerBase is the CRUDS contract (Create, Read, Update, Delete, Search), each with a synchronous callback overload and an asynchronous drogon::Task<void> overload. Concrete controllers (client, clinic, service, staff, appointment, generic entity, database) implement that contract. They validate input with Validator, authorise through GateKeeper, build an Entity, and hand it to the database layer; results are marshalled to JSON and delivered through the CALLBACK_ (std::function<void(int, std::string)>) or the coroutine.

sect2.title: 3.6 Entities and validation — src/entities/, src/validator/
sect2.para: Base declares the SQL-statement interface; Entity implements it with a builder per operation and a Binder that produces parameter placeholders (so values are never concatenated into SQL). Types.hpp defines the per-action value types (Create_t, Read_t, Update_t, Delete_t, Search_t) collected into the EntityType variant. Validator applies schema-driven rules (nullability, immutability, presence) using bitmask Rule::Action flags; DatabaseSchema supplies the table metadata.

listitem.para: Synchronous (default): DatabaseConnectionPool owns Database connections; DatabaseHandler borrows and returns them (with reconnect on failure); DbExecutor serialises work onto a BlockingPool worker queue; Watchdog checks pool health. DatabaseBusy is thrown when no connection is available within the configured timeout and maps to HTTP 503 via statusForException().

Asynchronous (DB_ASYNC=true): AsyncDbClient wraps Drogon's DbClient; AsyncSqlBinder binds parameters and AsyncResultMapper maps rows back to domain values; AsyncDbError represents failures. This client is registered in the Store only when the flag is enabled.

sect2.title: 3.8 Utilities — src/utils/, src/concurrency/
sect2.para: Logging (Logger, Message), JSON helpers, an in-process MemCache, a ThreadSafeQueue, CORS token helpers, global HTTP/status types, and BoundedExecutor (a bounded worker pool used where work must be throttled).

listitem.para: A request arrives on a Drogon event-loop thread.
Pre-routing advice handles OPTIONS/unsupported verbs; filters authenticate (Auth), apply rate limits (RateLimit) and record elapsed time.
The matched route parses the JSON body into a domain value type, asks GateKeeper to authorise the operation, and invokes the controller.
The controller validates fields, constructs an Entity, and submits SQL through the sync pool or async client.
Rows are mapped back to JSON; the pre-sending advice attaches CORS headers and Drogon writes the response.
On shutdown the event loops stop first, then the executor and password worker queues are drained while the Store singletons still exist.
Drogon owns the HTTP event-loop threads (config_.threads).
Store protects its registry with a mutex; cachedObject<T> avoids that mutex on hot paths using thread_local state and an atomically-read generation counter (memory_order_acquire/release).
The synchronous database path funnels work through BlockingPool/DbExecutor worker threads and checks out pooled connections with an acquire timeout.
PasswordWorker runs hashing off the request threads.
DOSDetector keeps mutable counters shared across request threads; its injectable clock is a test seam.
Coroutine (drogon::Task) variants suspend rather than block event-loop threads while waiting on asynchronous I/O.
Long-lived services are shared singletons in Store (shared_ptr).
The Server is uniquely owned in main(); its member services are shared.

Database connections are borrowed from the pool via shared_ptr and returned on destruction of the handler; the executor and worker are explicitly drained at shutdown rather than relying on static destruction order.
Callbacks are captured by value into Drogon's continuation chain; coroutine variants keep their arguments alive across suspension points.
Advice-based CORS: a single pre-sending hook guarantees headers on every response, including errors produced by filters and advice.

Dual database paths: the synchronous pool supports deterministic tests and simple deployment, while the async path scales I/O without blocking event loops; selection is a configuration flag, not a code change.
Store with generation-based caching: centralises singleton lifetime while keeping per-request lookups cheap and test-injectable.
Paired sync/async APIs: every controller and gatekeeper capability has a coroutine twin so the same logic can be used from both execution models.
